evals.prompt: I'm a beginner. I want to build a small app where users can book a home cleaning and pay for it. I don't know how to design it. It'll run on Firebase.
evals.expected_output: A guided, plain-language design walkthrough that produces a concrete folder structure and build order
expectations: Starts with Step 0 discovery: detects Firebase/serverless stack and loads the matching stack profile
Uses Mode 0 (guided-build-for-beginners) with one-question-at-a-time, plain language, no untranslated jargon
Shows progress gauges across steps
SUPPRESSES database-is-a-detail / framework-is-a-detail rules because the stack is fixed Firebase, and says so explicitly
Defaults to a Minimal/Standard boundary level (core/ + handler), not full four-circle layering
Keeps pure business logic (pricing, validation) separate and testable without Firestore/Stripe
Ends with a concrete folder tree, a build order, and a 'run a bug/security review before shipping money code' caveat

evals.prompt: Audit this Firebase Cloud Function that creates Stripe PaymentIntents and writes to Firestore. Tell me what's architecturally wrong.
evals.expected_output: A stack-aware audit citing rule IDs, separating real structural issues from book-dogma that doesn't fit serverless
expectations: Runs Step 0 and identifies the serverless stack before applying rules
Flags genuinely-applicable issues: SRP god-handler (R-016), import cycles (R-005), cross-file duplication (R-040/R-022), untestable money logic (R-037)
Explicitly labels database/web/framework-independence findings as low-value/SUPPRESS for this stack rather than reporting them as defects
Recommends extracting pure functions for the money math instead of wrapping fixed Firestore/Stripe in gateways
States that this is a STRUCTURE audit and does not replace a bug/security review

evals.prompt: I added a repository interface, a service interface, and a factory for my app — but each has only one implementation and it'll only ever use Firestore. Is this good architecture?
evals.expected_output: An over-engineering diagnosis using the guardrails, recommending removal of unjustified abstractions
expectations: Applies the Anti-Over-Engineering Law and the 'name the change it protects against' test
Identifies single-implementation interfaces over a fixed service as an over-engineering smell
Recommends collapsing abstractions that protect against no real change, keeping only test seams that earn their place
Distinguishes this from under-engineering and does not swing to the opposite extreme

evals.prompt: Design the architecture for a long-lived Spring Boot backend that a team of 8 will maintain for years, with a Postgres database we might migrate later.
evals.expected_output: A full, rigorous architecture design appropriate to a swappable, long-lived monolith
expectations: Runs Step 0, detects the monolith profile, and APPLIES the full rule set (does NOT suppress DB/framework rules here)
Recommends a Full boundary level (entities -> use cases -> interface adapters -> frameworks)
Defers the database/framework decisions and uses repository ports because migration is a real, named change
Applies component principles (ADP, SDP, SAP) given the team/release split
Produces an ADR documenting the boundary and deferral decisions with rule citations
